callouts.label: Mean Radiant Temperature
callouts.hint: Find the wall on the far left that is cold and frosty on one half and warm on the other, with wavy lines running from it to the person.
callouts.description: The area-weighted average temperature of the surfaces around a person. The body trades heat by radiation with every wall, window, and ceiling it faces, so a cold window chills someone even when the air is warm. Warm interior surfaces allow comfort at a lower air temperature (Chapter 4).
callouts.tip: Air temperature is what the thermostat reads. Radiant temperature is what the body feels.

callouts.label: Air Temperature
callouts.hint: Find the large wall thermometer on the upper left with a tall red column.
callouts.description: The dry-bulb temperature of the air around the occupant. It is the only variable a thermostat measures, and only at the thermostat's own location. Two rooms at the same air temperature can feel very different, which is why the other five variables matter.

callouts.label: Clothing Insulation
callouts.hint: Find the thick knit sweater draped over a chair at the lower left of the person.
callouts.description: Clothing is the personal layer of insulation, measured in clo. A heavy sweater lets a person feel comfortable in a cooler room, and shirtsleeves suit a warmer one. Dress codes and uniforms therefore change the room conditions people will accept (ASHRAE 55; Chapter 4).

callouts.label: Air Speed
callouts.hint: Find the set of curved teal wind lines blowing across the person's neck from a small ceiling vent on the upper right.
callouts.description: The rate of air movement at the occupant. Moving air carries heat away from skin, so a draft makes a cool room feel colder, while a gentle breeze can make a warm room feel better. Fans, supply diffusers, and open windows all change it (Chapter 14).

callouts.label: Metabolic Rate
callouts.hint: Find the pair of small figures on the lower right, one sitting still and one striding with a box.
callouts.description: The heat the body produces, which depends on activity and is measured in met. A person sitting quietly is about 1 met, and activity raises it. Someone carrying drywall in shirtsleeves needs a cooler room than someone sitting still in a sweater (Chapter 4).

callouts.label: Relative Humidity
callouts.hint: Find the round gauge with a big water droplet on its face on the far right.
callouts.description: Humidity sets how easily sweat evaporates from skin. Humid air makes warm conditions feel hotter and stickier, while the very dry indoor air of a Minnesota winter can dry skin and eyes (Chapter 4). Comfort standards weigh humidity along with temperature.

callouts.label: Cold Window, Normal Thermostat
callouts.hint: Find the lower-left scene of a shivering person beside a large frosty window, with a wall thermostat showing a mild setting.
callouts.description: Case 1: the thermostat shows an ordinary room temperature, yet the person beside a large cold window is chilly. The body loses heat by radiation to the cold glass, so the radiant temperature, not the air temperature, drives the feeling (Chapter 4's cold-window calculation).
callouts.tip: The cold window beat the thermostat.

callouts.label: The Occupant: A Heat Balance
callouts.hint: Find the seated figure in the middle, with a soft glow at the chest and faint wavy lines leaving the skin in several directions.
callouts.description: Comfort is a heat balance: the body makes heat and must lose it at about the same rate by radiation, convection, and evaporation. Fanger's PMV (Predicted Mean Vote) model, the standard method in ASHRAE 55, predicts the average vote of a large group from the six variables.

callouts.label: Hot Gym, Same Thermostat Setting
callouts.hint: Find the center-bottom scene of sweating people on exercise equipment, with a wall thermostat that matches the other scenes.
callouts.description: Case 2: a gym and a classroom share the same thermostat setting, but the gym feels too hot. People exercising make several times the heat of people sitting still, and they wear less, so metabolic rate and clothing change comfort even when the air temperature is identical.

callouts.label: The Seven-Point Sensation Scale
callouts.hint: Find the long strip along the bottom made of seven blocks that shift from deep blue on the left to deep red on the right.
callouts.description: ASHRAE 55 uses a seven-point scale: cold (-3), cool (-2), slightly cool (-1), neutral (0), slightly warm (+1), warm (+2), and hot (+3). PMV is the predicted mean vote of a large group on this scale, and the standard treats a result near neutral as acceptable.

callouts.label: Open Windows in Summer
callouts.hint: Find the lower-right scene of relaxed people in light clothes in a room with wide-open windows and a sunny summer garden outside.
callouts.description: Case 3: in a naturally ventilated room in summer, where people can open windows and adjust clothing, occupants accept a warmer range than in a sealed air-conditioned room. The Brager and de Dear adaptive model links acceptable indoor temperature to the outdoor climate. ASHRAE 55 allows it only for occupant-controlled spaces without mechanical cooling.
